setup.zh: 外门执事周衡给新弟子发东西：灰袍，木牌，三块灵石——「每人交一块，给外门的『公中』。」马小宝冲你笑，笑得像他爹。
setup.en: Zhou Heng, steward of the outer court, hands out a grey robe, a wooden tag and three spirit stones — "one each goes to the outer court's common fund." Ma Xiaobao smiles at you, just like his father.

recap.zh: 外门的第一夜：周衡发下三块灵石，马小宝要收一块「公中」。
recap.en: The first night in the outer court: Zhou Heng handed out three spirit stones, and Ma Xiaobao wanted one for his "common fund."

zh: 一件灰袍，一块木牌，三块灵石。
en: A grey robe, a wooden tag, three spirit stones.
"One each, for the outer court's common fund."

story.zh:
那天傍晚，新入门的弟子许到山门外头，跟送考的家里人说一句话，一炷香为限。

小满从木架上取回了爷爷那张弓——第三排左数第七个，一个手指头也没人碰过——背在背上，跑到山门外头。石阶底下，人已散了大半，剩下的，三三两两，有的在哭，有的在笑，有的蹲在地上，拿树枝在泥地里画着什么。

舅舅站在那儿。他站在头一级石阶的边上，仰着脸，也不知站了多久，青布长衫的下摆全是泥。他一看见小满，先不问考上没考上，先问：「饿不饿？」

小满道：「饿。」

舅舅从包袱里摸出最后半张饼，塞进他手里，这才问：「……考上了？」

小满道：「外门。」

舅舅一把抓住了他的胳膊，抓得死紧。他转过身，对着旁边一个不认识的老头，大声道：「我外甥！考上了！三百级，一口气！」那老头吓了一跳。舅舅又对着另一个不认识的妇人道：「我外甥！」那妇人也吓了一跳。舅舅又道：「当年，我也爬到了一百八十级——」

小满道：「舅舅。」

舅舅道：「……一百六十级。」

小满道：「舅舅。一百六十级那里，崖壁上刻满了字。」

舅舅道：「嗯。」

小满道：「都是在那一级上坐下过的人刻的。」

舅舅不说话了。他把脸转过去，朝着泗水那边，看了很久。小满看见他的肩膀动了一下。

小满道：「舅舅，我替你走上来了。」

舅舅没有回头。过了好一会儿，他才开口，声音有点哑，道：「……风大。」

他拿袖子在脸上抹了一把，又抹了一把，然后转回来，把小满背上那张弓扶正了，把他的衣领翻好——翻衣领的那一下，同他姐姐一模一样——道：「回去吧。一炷香到了。」

那天夜里，舅舅没有再提他外甥一个字。后来兖州那个爹问他：「老哥，你当年，到底爬到了多少级？」舅舅想了一想，道：「一百六十级。」

那是他这辈子，头一回，没有多说十级。

那天晚上，外门执事周衡给新弟子发东西。

周衡是个三十来岁的瘦高个儿，一脸愁苦，腋下永远夹着一本厚得能当枕头使的账簿，发一样东西，便往账簿上记一笔。他发的是两样：一件灰袍，一块木牌。每发一个人，他都要抬头看那人一眼，道一声：「有前途！」发给金单灵根的，他说「有前途！」；发给四灵根色杂的，他也说「有前途！」；发给孙二狗，他看了半天，还是说了一声「有前途！」，只是声音小了些。

轮到马小宝，周衡看了看名册上「荐书」那两个字，嘴唇动了一动，那三个字到底没说出口。

轮到小满，他看了看名册上「五行杂灵根」那几个字，抬起头来，端详了小满好一会儿，道：「……有前途。」没有那个叹号。木牌是外门弟子的腰牌，枣木的，巴掌大，一面刻「沉鼎」，一面刻各人的名字。

小满捧着那块腰牌，又摸了摸胸口那块狐纹木牌，忍不住笑了一笑。他进山的时候，胸口挂一块木牌；进了山门，腰上又挂一块木牌。一块是给他发工钱的，一块是欠他一张饼的。两块都是木头，两块他都得好好收着。

周衡发完了东西，清了清嗓子，照着账簿念道：「灵石，一个月三块，明日一早到执事房领，往后每月初一领。领了之后，外门的规矩——」念到这里，他的眼睛往旁边瞟了一下，声音也低了下去，「每人交一块，给马师兄……咳，给外门的『公中』。」

新弟子们面面相觑。有人小声问：「马师兄是谁？」

原来这「公中」，是外门的老规矩，从来是几个入门三五年的老弟子管着，说是替大家置办灯油、修补屋瓦，至于置办了没有、修补了没有，谁也没见过。这一日午后，马家的家丁在山下的镇上，请那几个老弟子吃了一顿酒；吃完了酒，马小宝便成了「马师兄」，成了管公中的人。前后不过两个时辰。

小满看了看马小宝。马小宝站在周衡身后，正冲他笑，笑得跟他爹马三在门框上敲短棍的时候一模一样。他手里又是一块桂花糕，咬了一口，腮帮子一鼓一鼓的。
story.en:
Toward evening that day the new disciples were allowed out of the gate to say a word to the family who'd brought them, for the length of one stick of incense.

Xiaoman took his grandfather's bow back from the rack — third row, seventh from the left, not a finger laid on it — slung it on his back, and ran out of the gate. At the foot of the stair the crowd had mostly gone; those left, in twos and threes, some crying, some laughing, some crouched drawing in the mud with a twig.

His uncle stood there. He stood at the edge of the first step, face turned up, who knew how long, the hem of his blue gown all mud. The moment he saw Xiaoman, before asking whether he'd got in, he asked: "Hungry?"

Xiaoman said, "Hungry."

His uncle took the last half flatbread from his bundle and pressed it into his hand, and only then asked: "…Got in?"

Xiaoman said, "Outer court."

His uncle seized his arm, gripping it hard. He turned to an old man he didn't know and said loudly: "My nephew! He got in! Three hundred steps, one breath!" The old man jumped. His uncle said to a woman he didn't know: "My nephew!" The woman jumped too. His uncle said: "Back then, I got to step one hundred and eighty —"

Xiaoman said, "Uncle."

His uncle said: "…One hundred and sixty."

Xiaoman said, "Uncle. At step one hundred and sixty the cliff wall's covered in carving."

His uncle said, "Mm."

Xiaoman said, "It's all people who sat down on that step."

His uncle stopped talking. He turned his face toward the Si River and looked a long time. Xiaoman saw his shoulders move.

Xiaoman said, "Uncle, I walked up for you."

His uncle didn't turn round. After a good while he spoke, his voice a little hoarse: "…Windy."

He wiped his face with his sleeve, and wiped it again; then turned back, set the bow straight on Xiaoman's back, turned his collar straight — that turn of the collar exactly like his sister's — and said: "Go on back. The incense is out."

That night his uncle didn't mention his nephew again. Later the Yanzhou father asked him: "Old brother, back then, how many steps did you really get to?" His uncle thought and said: "A hundred and sixty."

It was the first time in his life he hadn't added ten.

That evening the outer-court steward, Zhou Heng, handed out things to the new disciples.

Zhou Heng was a tall thin man of thirty-odd with a long-suffering face, forever with a ledger under his arm thick enough to use as a pillow; each thing he handed out, he entered a line. He handed out two things: a grey robe and a wooden token. With each person he looked up once and said: "Promising!" To the metal single-root, "Promising!"; to the muddy four-root, "Promising!"; to Sun Ergou, after looking a long time, still "Promising!" — only quieter.

At Ma Xiaobao, Zhou Heng looked at the words *letter of recommendation* in the register; his lips moved, but the word never came out.

At Xiaoman, he looked at *mixed five-element root* in the register, looked up, studied Xiaoman a good while, and said: "…Promising." Without the exclamation mark. The wooden token was an outer disciple's waist tag, jujube wood, palm-sized, one side carved *Chending*, the other each person's name.

Xiaoman held the waist tag, touched the fox-carved token at his chest, and couldn't help smiling. Coming up the mountain he'd had one wooden token at his chest; through the gate, another at his waist. One would pay him wages; the other owed him a flatbread. Both were wood, and both he'd have to keep safe.

The handing-out done, Zhou Heng cleared his throat and read from the ledger: "Spirit stones: three a month. Collect at the stewards' office first thing tomorrow, and on the first of every month after. Once collected, the outer court's rule —" here his eyes slid sideways and his voice dropped, "— each gives one to Senior Brother Ma… ahem, to the outer court's 'common fund'."

The new disciples looked at one another. Someone asked quietly, "Who's Senior Brother Ma?"

This "common fund" was an old outer-court rule, always run by a few old disciples three or five years in, said to buy lamp oil and patch the roof tiles; whether any oil was bought or any tiles patched, nobody had ever seen. That afternoon the Mas' servants had treated those old disciples to a meal of wine in the town below; the wine drunk, Ma Xiaobao became "Senior Brother Ma", the one in charge of the common fund. Two hours, start to finish.

Xiaoman looked at Ma Xiaobao. Ma Xiaobao stood behind Zhou Heng grinning at him, a grin exactly like his father Ma San's rapping his club on a doorframe. Another osmanthus cake in his hand; he took a bite, cheeks bulging.

exits.means: pays the one stone to the common fund, keeps the peace for now

refuse.en: You have no spirit stones on you.

what.zh: 外门的「公中」：收了你一块灵石。
what.en: The outer court's "common fund": took one of your spirit stones.

story.zh:
小满什么也没说。他从怀里摸出一块灵石，交了。马小宝掂了一掂，冲他笑，笑得跟他爹一模一样。

他心里却记了一笔：公中，一块。马小宝。
story.en:
Xiaoman said nothing. He took a spirit stone from his jacket and handed it over. Ma Xiaobao weighed it in his palm and grinned at him, a grin exactly like his father's.

But in his heart he entered a line: Common fund, one stone. Ma Xiaobao.

exits.means: refuses to pay the common fund

story.zh:
小满什么也没说，也没有交。他把怀里的灵石一块一块放进他娘给的那个空钱袋里，叮，叮，叮。空钱袋里，头一回有了东西。

他知道往后会怎样：马小宝不会当着周衡的面动手，他会等。他爹就是这么收租的——先笑，再等，等你以为没事了，门就飞了。那就等。
story.en:
Xiaoman said nothing, and didn't hand anything over either. He put the spirit stones from his jacket one by one into the empty purse his mother had given him — *ting, ting, ting*. For the first time, the empty purse held something.

He knew what would come of it: Ma Xiaobao wouldn't lift a hand in front of Zhou Heng; he'd wait. That was how his father collected rent — grin first, then wait, wait till you think it's over, and then the door flies. Then let him wait.
